value.overview: The Rose-throated Becard is a stocky, large-headed songbird of the tropical Americas. It is named for the rose-pink throat patch shown by males of many populations, although males in some wetter regions, including parts of Costa Rica, may lack obvious pink. The species usually remains quiet in the forest canopy, where it searches for insects and small fruits. It often occurs in forest edges, open woodland, river corridors, and second-growth habitats as well as more continuous forest.
value.classification: The Rose-throated Becard belongs to the family Tityridae, which includes becards, tityras, and related birds. Its scientific name is Pachyramphus aglaiae.
value.identification: This becard is about 16–18 cm long, with a broad bill, large head, and a conspicuous dark, peaked crown. Adult males are generally gray, with darker upperparts and often a rose-colored throat or neck bib. Females are browner, with rusty or brown upperparts, pale underparts, and a dark crown. Young birds resemble females. Plumage varies geographically, and Costa Rican birds may show little or no pink on the throat, so shape, crown, and behavior are useful identification features.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from the southwestern United States through Mexico and Central America to western Panama, with Costa Rica forming the southern part of its regular breeding range. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in the northern and western lowlands and foothills, including areas around the Gulf of Nicoya, but records also extend into other suitable regions. It uses dry and moist forest, woodland, forest edges, shaded plantations, riparian growth, savanna trees, and second-growth vegetation, generally favoring tall trees and open canopy structure.
value.migrationStatus: Rose-throated Becards in Costa Rica include resident breeding populations, especially in the north and west, as well as seasonal visitors from farther north. Northern migrants generally arrive during the wet-season-to-dry-season transition, from about October, and may remain through the dry season before departing in spring. Local movements and timing vary by region and population.
value.breeding: Breeding information is better documented outside Costa Rica than within the country. The species builds a large, bulky, rounded or globular nest from plant fibers and other vegetation, usually suspended from a tree branch and equipped with a small entrance. The female typically lays several pale eggs marked with brown. The female performs most or all incubation, while both adults feed the young. In Costa Rica, breeding is associated with the resident populations rather than the mainly seasonal northern migrants.
value.dietFeeding: The Rose-throated Becard eats mostly insects and other small arthropods, including insects picked from leaves and twigs. It also takes small fruits and occasionally seeds. It commonly forages high in the canopy or subcanopy, sitting quietly before making short flights to glean prey from foliage or catch insects in the air. In Costa Rica it may be seen alone or in pairs in forest edges, open woodland, and fruiting trees.
value.behavior: This species is usually unobtrusive and spends much of its time perched motionless in the upper or middle canopy. It often makes short sallies from a lookout perch and may briefly hover while taking prey from foliage. Individuals commonly forage singly or in pairs, although they can sometimes join mixed-species feeding groups. The large head, heavy bill, dark crown, and deliberate movements are characteristic when the bird is observed in good light.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered threatened, although precise population estimates and long-term trends are limited.
